client: I've been really stressed lately about this family reunion that's coming up next month. Just thinking about it makes my heart race — like, I can feel my chest tighten up and I start dreading it days in advance. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to help, honestly, because the situation with my cousin is pretty complicated and I don't see how just... talking changes any of that.
therapist: It sounds like even just bringing this up carries a real weight for you — your voice and words both carry that tension, like this has been sitting heavily on you for a while. Your skepticism about talking makes complete sense, especially when the situation feels tangled and unresolved — that's actually a really honest and important thing to name. What I'd gently offer is that while we can't change your cousin or the circumstances, we *can* work on how your mind is responding to the anticipation, because that dread building up days in advance is something we have real tools to address together.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I guess that's a fair point — like, the dread itself is its own separate thing from whatever actually happens at the reunion. But I'm not totally convinced, because when I try to just "not think about it," that never works, it just kind of bounces back harder. I don't know what these tools even are, so I'm a little skeptical they'd actually work for someone like me.
therapist: You're actually describing something really well-documented — that "don't think about it" strategy tends to backfire, and the fact that you've noticed that pattern in yourself shows real self-awareness. Your voice has this quality of someone working hard to stay measured while carrying genuine uncertainty, which makes sense — it's reasonable to be skeptical of something you haven't tried yet. What I want you to know is that CBT doesn't ask you to suppress thoughts; it's more about examining *what those thoughts are actually telling you* and whether they hold up under scrutiny, which is a very different thing.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: Okay, so examining the thoughts rather than pushing them away — that does sound different from what I've been doing. But I'm a little worried that when I actually look at what I'm thinking about my cousin, it's going to feel really overwhelming, like opening a door I've been keeping shut for a reason. What if looking at it more closely just makes the anxiety worse instead of better?
therapist: The way you're speaking right now — quietly, carefully — really reflects that sense of standing at a threshold you're not sure you want to cross, and that caution deserves respect, not pressure. That fear of being overwhelmed is actually one of the most common things people bring to this work, and it's worth knowing that we wouldn't fling that door open all at once — we'd approach it gradually, at a pace that feels manageable for you. And often, what's behind the door turns out to be more bearable in small, examined pieces than it is as one looming, shapeless dread.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, very quiet, moderate-paced speech

client: That actually makes me feel a little less panicked about the idea, knowing it wouldn't be all at once. I think part of what I've been avoiding is this specific thing my cousin said to me at the last reunion — it's been sitting in my chest like a stone ever since, and I've just been carrying it around without really looking at it. I'm not sure I even know how to start examining it without just... spiraling into all the feelings again.
therapist: The way you're speaking — softly, carefully, with that quiet weight in your voice — really matches what you're describing, like you're holding something fragile and heavy at the same time. A good place to start isn't with the feelings the memory brings up, but with something more concrete: just the thought itself — what did your mind make that comment *mean* about you? That small distinction, between what your cousin said and the story your mind built around it, is often where we find the most useful thread to pull.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: Okay, when I really try to sit with that question... I think what my mind made it mean is that I'm someone who doesn't really belong in my own family, like I'm always slightly on the outside looking in. That's a really uncomfortable thing to say out loud, actually, and I'm not sure I believe it's just a "story" — it feels more like evidence of something that's actually true about me. How do you separate what's a thought from what's just... reality?
therapist: The way you're speaking right now — quickly, with that higher pitch — tells me that naming this out loud landed somewhere real and tender, even as you're trying to process it carefully. What you've just done takes real courage, and I want to gently point out that the very fact this belief feels like *reality* rather than a thought is actually one of the most important things CBT works with — because the thoughts that feel most like facts are usually the ones that have never been examined or challenged. So the question worth sitting with is: what would you need to look at to actually *test* whether you don't belong, rather than just assuming the feeling is proof?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: That question is making me uncomfortable in a way I didn't expect, because part of me is realizing I've never actually looked for evidence that I do belong — I've only ever collected the moments that confirmed I don't. But testing it feels risky, like if I actually look and the evidence still points to not belonging, then I can't even have the comfort of uncertainty anymore. I guess I'm scared that examining it will just make the conclusion more solid, not less.
therapist: The softness in your voice right now, paired with something that sounds almost fragile in your tone, tells me this realization is landing somewhere really deep and tender — and what you've just described is genuinely one of the most important insights a person can have about themselves. You've named something called *confirmation bias* almost perfectly: when we only collect the evidence that confirms our fears, the verdict always feels inevitable, but that's not because the case is closed — it's because we've been working as the prosecutor and never the defense. The discomfort you're feeling right now isn't a sign this is too dangerous to look at; it's actually a sign that something real and important is starting to shift.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: The prosecutor and defense thing actually lands for me — I can see how I've been building a one-sided case against myself for years. But I'm not sure I even know what the defense evidence would look like, because the moments where I did feel included always seem to have some asterisk attached, like "they were just being polite" or "that doesn't really count." How do I know when I'm genuinely reconsidering the evidence versus just talking myself into feeling better temporarily?
therapist: The way you're speaking — with that high, careful pitch and measured pace — suggests you're working really hard to think this through clearly even while something underneath still feels unsettled, and that tension is actually really meaningful here. What you've just described — the asterisk, the "that doesn't count" — is the defense attorney getting immediately overruled, and noticing that pattern *is* the work; you're not just talking yourself into feeling better, you're catching your mind in the act of dismissing evidence unfairly. The difference between genuine reconsideration and temporary comfort is exactly this: real reconsideration feels uncomfortable and uncertain, not reassuring — and right now, you're clearly doing the harder thing.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: That actually helps me trust what I'm feeling right now a little more, because it does feel uncomfortable and uncertain rather than like some neat resolution. But I'm already thinking ahead to the reunion itself, and I'm worried that even if I start to see the evidence differently in here, in the moment when my cousin is actually in front of me, all of this is just going to fly out the window. It's one thing to think clearly when I'm sitting here talking to you, and another thing entirely when the anxiety kicks in and I'm standing in my aunt's backyard trying not to look like I don't belong.
therapist: The speed and pitch in your voice right now really reflects that forward-rushing anxiety, like your mind is already standing in that backyard even while you're here — and that's actually really important information, because it means we can work with the *reunion situation specifically*, not just the abstract idea of it. What you're describing is one of the most common and valid concerns people have, and the answer isn't to rely on remembering insights in the moment, but to practice them enough beforehand that they become more automatic — almost like rehearsing a different way of seeing, so it's more available to you under pressure. The goal isn't to be perfectly clear-headed when your cousin is in front of you; it's to have just enough of a foothold to pause for one second before the old story takes over completely.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: Just one second of pause — that actually feels more achievable than what I was imagining, which was somehow staying completely calm and rational the whole time. But I'm not sure what "practicing" this actually looks like in real life, like am I supposed to just... imagine the reunion over and over until it feels less scary? Because I've tried picturing stressful situations before and it usually just makes me more anxious, not less.
therapist: The brightness and slight tension in your voice tells me there's something hopeful trying to emerge here, even while a real concern is pushing back — and that concern is valid, because what you've tried before, just replaying the stressful scene, is actually different from what I'm describing. Rather than imagining the reunion until it feels less scary, the practice is more specific: rehearsing that one-second pause by connecting it to a single grounding thought, like "I'm only collecting half the evidence," so that thought becomes a reflex you can reach for rather than a concept you have to remember. It's less about desensitizing yourself to the scene and more about building one small, reliable handhold for when the anxiety spikes.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: A single grounding thought as a reflex — okay, that does sound more manageable than what I was picturing. I guess my worry is that in that moment, "I'm only collecting half the evidence" might feel too abstract, like my brain won't be able to grab onto something that sounds so... clinical, when everything is emotionally charged. Is it okay if the thought is something that feels more personal to me, or does it need to be that specific phrasing?
therapist: The softness and careful pace in your voice right now feels like someone who is genuinely trying to make this work for themselves rather than just going through the motions — and the fact that you're already thinking about what will actually land for *you* in that moment is exactly the right instinct. Not only is it okay for the thought to feel personal, it's actually more effective that way — the grounding thought works best when it carries your own meaning and texture, not mine. So what we could do together is find the phrasing that feels true and reachable to you, something that captures the same idea but in words that sound like you rather than a textbook.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech
